e: Which district did the oil come from? The database of amphora inscriptions

The database of the CEIPAC research group in Barcelona (Roman Open Data) records 48,059 inscribed amphorae from the whole empire; 14,051 of them were found in Rome, 12,120 of these around Monte Testaccio. 88% of the amphorae from Rome are Baetican oil amphorae (Dressel 20). The amphorae from Rome carry 7,459 stamps, 10,938 painted inscriptions and 1,424 scratched marks in the database.
The γ line, the weight of the oil, can be read in full on 348 amphorae from Rome. The most frequent value is 216 Roman pounds (on 157 amphorae) and the median is 215 pounds: roughly 70 kg of oil.

The δ line opens with the place of control: the name of the district of Baetica where the oil was weighed and registered. 2,190 δ inscriptions are known from Rome, but the name of the district can be read on only 424 amphorae; 318 of these can be dated by the names of the consuls or by the excavated layer.

In the mid-2nd century all three large districts appear, with Astigi leading (46%). Under Marcus Aurelius and Commodus most inscriptions name Hispalis and Corduba. Under the Severans the picture is reversed: 75% of the inscriptions preserving a district name are from Astigi. Almost all of these are entries beginning “R Astigis arca…”, referring to the imperial treasury, so the share partly shows that the office at Astigi wrote out its name most consistently. The numbers are small and also depend on which part of the mound the excavation reached: the table describes the surviving and excavated inscriptions, not the whole import.

The stamp ties the amphora to the pottery that made it. Of the 6,602 stamps on Dressel 20 amphorae from Rome, 3,078 can be tied to a single pottery identified on the banks of the Guadalquivir (Baetis) and the Genil (72 potteries); a further 914 stamps occur at more than one pottery. 51% of the identified stamps come from potteries of the district of Hispalis, 30% from that of Corduba and 18% from that of Astigi. The district is given in brackets beside the bars; the potteries appear under their modern names. La Catria, which supplied the most stamps found in Rome, lies near Lora del Río.
From which year?

4,714 amphorae from Rome can be dated to a single year: 555 by the consular date written on them, 4,159 by the excavated layer. Most amphorae come from these years: 145 (1,033), 149 (186), 160 (149), 161 (132), 174 (270), 177 (121), 179 (841), 207 (125), 208 (177), 214 (266), 216 (124), 246 (118), 254 (439). This is not a fluctuation of imports: each part of the mound holds the refuse of different years, and the numbers show which years’ layers research has reached (Dressel’s collecting in the 19th century and the Spanish excavation under way since 1989). The database dates one amphora to 256, but the pair of consuls written on it (Valerianus II and Lucillus) belongs to 265; we corrected this.
